extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers, literary students, and critics (writers working on novels/longer fiction)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on choosing and handling narrative perspective in the novel: when to use first-person/autobiography, third-person dramatization, or epistolary forms; how to dramatize a character's consciousness; and how to balance dramatic method with economy. Uses examples (Meredith, Dickens, Henry James, Dostoevsky, Richardson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of a personal narrator
rubrics_metrics.description: A personal narrator (first-person/autobiography) will do very well and may be extremely helpful so long as the story is only the reflection of life beyond and outside him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use first-person when the tale chiefly reports the world outside the narrator and the narrator functions as an onlooker/recorder. Examples: Copperfield and Esmond function well as personal narrators when the subject is not essentially their inner life. Anti-pattern: relying on a personal narrator when the main weight of the story is the narrator’s own inward drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation of autobiography when the story centers on the narrator's inner life
rubrics_metrics.description: When the story begins to find its centre of gravity in the narrator’s own life, his report of himself becomes inadequate; 'the dramatizing force of the first person gives out.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the chief question of the book is 'what it was like to be X' (the narrator), autobiography is likely to fall short because the narrator can only report and recall, not put his present consciousness before the reader. Example: Meredith’s Harry Richmond—his first-person account cannot fully render the inner history demanded by the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer dramatization of consciousness to retrospective account
rubrics_metrics.description: Drama we want, always drama, for the central, essential, paramount affair; the narrator’s consciousness ought to be dramatized. Something is lost if it is represented solely by his account of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, make a character’s inner life visible and active in the narrative (showing rather than telling). Example: Dostoevsky’s Crime and Punishment immerses the reader in Raskolnikov’s experience so the reader 'becomes Raskolnikov.' Anti-pattern: relying on a narrator’s retrospective summary when immediacy and conviction require dramatisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using third-person to dramatize the hero's mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Return to third person not by resuming the author’s original part, but by showing the man in the act of judging and reflecting—his consciousness appears in the act of agitation and becomes 'a spectacle for the reader.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Third-person can be used to render the hero’s consciousness dramatized on the page: we still see the scene through his eyes, but we also see his mind at work. This method gives the reader direct access to the mind without relying on the narrator’s after-the-fact report (examples: Henry James’s technique in The Ambassadors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial withdrawal (let the mind/scene speak)
rubrics_metrics.description: The author should withdraw so that the book 'looks poor and thin' if the author openly claims it; better to father the fiction upon another and then move further away until the author 'vanishes and leaves his people to act the story.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from interposing the author's own explanatory vision; allow the scene, the behavior, and the surface of thought to supply meaning. Example: Henry James makes Strether’s mind tell its story by images of thought rather than authorial exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of thought through surface images and movements
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist represents a mind by means of the movement that flickers over the surface of it: 'The impulses and reactions of his mood are the players upon the new scene.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To dramatize thought, show successive immediate images, impulses, ripples of attention and feeling—small scenes of the mind—rather than summarizing its content. This preserves suspense and theatrical effect while making inner change visible to the reader (example: The Ambassadors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid giving privileged authorial knowledge (suspend full exposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the author begins to expound the substance of a character’s thought, he must at once give the whole of it; better to withhold and let the mind's surface appearances unfold gradually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the reader in the position of spectator rather than confederate of the author. This allows 'deliberation, refrainment, suspension' like drama on stage and avoids spoiling mysteries (example: in a tale of murder, the murderer cannot narrate without betraying the secret).

rubrics_metrics.name: Method selection guided by the subject (twofold consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any story there is an ideal point on the line of progress towards drama where the author finds the right method; the choice is indicated by the subject itself and guided by a twofold consideration: drama and economy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide how far to dramatize based on what the subject needs to speak for itself, and balance this against economy—don’t dramatize further than the subject profits by it. Examples: prefer dramatization when the subject requires immediacy; abstain if it would displace or obscure the subject (David Copperfield illustrates economy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy: do not over-treat the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: The method is to be pushed as far as the subject can profit by it, but no further. A story is damaged by too much treatment as by too little.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid adding gratuitous psychological dramatization that shifts the centre of gravity or overcomplicates the narrative. Example: Dickens could have dramatized David’s mind but would have displaced the subject, which is the linked fortunes of people around David.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of epistolary form to dramatize ongoing emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: The epistolary novel is engaged in the attempt to show a mind in action and to get into the closest touch with a character’s life: 'Reading her letters, you hear the cry that was wrung from her at the moment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use letters/diary fragments to keep emotion contemporaneous and immediate (Clarissa as example). Beware practical drawbacks and strained verisimilitude (characters kept at a distance so communication by letter remains plausible; the method can be impracticable for large-scale enterprise).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let the narrator stand between reader and active mind
rubrics_metrics.description: No reflection, no picture, where living drama is possible: 'do not let the hero come between us and his active mind, do not let the heroine stand in front of her emotions and portray them—unless for cause.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unless there is a deliberate effect achieved by the narrator’s presence (e.g., Barry Lyndon’s self-revelation), prioritize techniques that place the reader in direct relation to the character's mental action. If the narrator’s mediation is necessary for effect, keep it purposeful and evident.
